q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which the Napoleonic Wars contributed to independence movements in Latin America.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why creoles led the independence movements rather than other social groups, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the new Latin American republics continued colonial-era social hierarchies after independence.

sample_answers.a: When Napoleon invaded Spain and deposed the Spanish king in 1808, colonial officials lost their legitimate source of authority; American-born elites argued that sovereignty reverted to the people and used the crisis to establish juntas that soon declared independence.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, creoles had education, wealth, and administrative experience but were blocked from the highest offices reserved for peninsulares, so they had both the capacity to organize revolutions and a direct grievance against Spanish rule.
sample_answers.c: Independence leaders preserved slavery in most new republics and kept land concentrated in the hands of a small elite, so indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans, and the poor remained subordinated just as under colonial rule.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain Latin American independence as a movement led primarily by creoles — American-born people of Spanish descent — who combined Enlightenment ideals with concrete grievances. Creoles resented the peninsulares, Spanish-born officials who monopolized high colonial offices, and they chafed under mercantilist restrictions that limited their trade. The decisive opening came when Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 shattered imperial authority; with the king deposed, creoles argued that sovereignty returned to the American peoples. Yet the revolutions they led were socially conservative: while they adopted the language of liberty and constitutions, most independence leaders preserved slavery and left the colonial hierarchy of land and labor largely intact, ensuring that political independence did not mean social revolution.
—Historian's account of Latin American independence in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE reason Bolívar gives for why Spanish Americans should seek independence.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Bolívar characterizes the position of Spanish Americans.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Bolívar believed unity among the new states was necessary.

sample_answers.a: Bolívar argues that reconciliation between America and Spain is impossible — ‘the hatred that the Peninsula has inspired in us is greater than the ocean between us’ — so that separation, not continued union, is the only resolution.
sample_answers.b: He describes Spanish Americans as caught between worlds — neither fully European nor fully American — a people with their own distinct identity forged by three centuries of colonial experience.
sample_answers.c: Bolívar believed that divided, the new republics would be weak and vulnerable to reconquest by Spain or domination by other powers; only a united front could secure their independence and give them weight in the world.

q2.stimulus:
We are not Europeans, we are not Indians, but an intermediate species between the aborigines and the Spaniards. Americans by birth and Europeans by law, we find ourselves engaged in a dual conflict: we dispute with the natives for titles of ownership, and we maintain ourselves in the country where we were born against the opposition of the invaders. ... The hatred that the Peninsula has inspired in us is greater than the ocean between us. ... It would be easier to have the two continents meet than to reconcile the spirits of the two countries.
—Adapted from Simón Bolívar, Letter from Jamaica, 1815

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the portrait that presents Bolívar as a republican leader rather than a monarch.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which portraits like this one served the political goals of new Latin American republics.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between Bolívar's vision for Spanish America and the actual political outcome by 1830.

sample_answers.a: Bolívar is shown in a military uniform without crown, throne, or other royal regalia, presenting him as a citizen-general whose authority derives from the revolutionary cause rather than hereditary right.
sample_answers.b: Portraits of independence heroes gave the new republics visual symbols of legitimacy and national identity, helping diverse populations see themselves as citizens of a shared nation rather than subjects of a distant king.
sample_answers.c: Bolívar dreamed of a united Spanish America (and briefly led the federation of Gran Colombia), but by 1830 the region had fragmented into separate rival republics, and Gran Colombia itself dissolved as Venezuela and Ecuador broke away.

q3.stimulus: The image is an 1825 portrait of Simón Bolívar by the Peruvian artist José Gil de Castro, painted during the wars of independence. Bolívar, known as the Liberator, led the independence movements that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia from Spanish rule. The portrait shows him in military uniform, and such images were widely circulated to build support for the revolutionary cause and the new republics.
